l: Sumer
Sumer is the earliest known <color=#3366CC>civilization</color>, located in the historical region of southern <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> (now south-central
<color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>), emerging during the <color=#3366CC>Chalcolithic</color> and <color=#3366CC>early Bronze</color> Ages between the 5th and 4th millennium BC. Like nearby

<color=#3366CC>Elam</color>, it is one of the <color=#3366CC>cradles of civilization</color>, along with <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley</color>, the Erligang culture of the Yellow River

valley, <color=#3366CC>Caral-Supe</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Mesoamerica</color>. Living along the valleys of the <color=#3366CC>Tigris</color> and <color=#3366CC>Euphrates</color> rivers, Sumerian farmers
grew an abundance of grain and other crops, a surplus of which enabled them to form urban settlements. The world's
earliest known texts come from the Sumerian cities of <color=#3366CC>Uruk</color> and Jemdet Nasr, and date to between c. 3350 – c. 2500
BC, following a period of <color=#3366CC>proto-writing</color> c. 4000 – c. 2500 BC.
Name
The term "Sumer" comes from the <color=#3366CC>Akkadian</color> name for the "Sumerians", the ancient non-<color=#3366CC>Semitic</color>-speaking inhabitants of
southern <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>. In their inscriptions, the Sumerians called their land "Kengir", the "Country of the noble lords",
and their language "Emegir" ( or eme-gi15).
The Akkadians, the East Semitic-speaking people who later conquered the Sumerian <color=#3366CC>city-states</color>, gave Sumer its main
historical name, but the <color=#3366CC>phonological</color> development of the term šumerû is uncertain. Hebrew Šinar, <color=#3366CC>Egyptian</color> Sngr, and
<color=#3366CC>Hittite</color> Šanhar(a), all referring to southern Mesopotamia, could potentailly be western variants of Sumer.
Origins
Most historians have suggested that Sumer was first permanently settled between c. 5500 and c. 3300 BC by a <color=#3366CC>West</color>
<color=#3366CC>Asian</color> people who spoke the <color=#3366CC>Sumerian language</color> (pointing to the names of cities, rivers, basic occupations, etc., as
evidence), a non-Semitic and non-<color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color> agglutinative <color=#3366CC>language isolate</color>.
Others have suggested that the Sumerians were a <color=#3366CC>North African</color> people who migrated from the Green Sahara into the
<color=#3366CC>Middle East</color> and were responsible for the spread of farming in the Middle East. However, contrary evidence strongly
suggests that the first farming originated in the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color>. Although not specifically discussing Sumerians,
Lazaridis et al. 2016 have suggested a mix of basal Eurasian and western Eurasian hunter-gatherer ancestry for the
pre-Semitic peoples of the fertile crescent, particularly the <color=#3366CC>Natufians</color>, after testing the genomes of Natufian and other
<color=#3366CC>Pre-Pottery Neolithic</color> culture-bearers.
Some scholars associate the Sumerians with the <color=#3366CC>Hurrians</color> and <color=#3366CC>Urartians</color>, and suggest the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> as their homeland.
This is not generally accepted.
Based on mentions of <color=#3366CC>Dilmun</color> as the "home city of the land of Sumer" in Sumerian legends and literature, other
scholars have suggested the possibility that the Sumerians originated from Dilmun, which was theorized to be the
island of <color=#3366CC>Bahrain</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color>. In Sumerian mythology, Dilmun was also mentioned as the home of deities such
as <color=#3366CC>Enki</color>. The status of Dilmun as the Sumerians' ancestral homeland has not been established, but archaeologists have
found evidence of civilization in Bahrain, namely the existence of Mesopotamian-style round disks.
A prehistoric people who lived in the region before the Sumerians have been termed the "Proto-Euphrateans" or
"<color=#3366CC>Ubaidians</color>", and are theorized to have evolved from the Samarra culture of northern Mesopotamia. The Ubaidians,
though never mentioned by the Sumerians themselves, are assumed by modern-day scholars to have been the first
civilizing force in Sumer. They drained the marshes for <color=#3366CC>agriculture</color>, developed trade, and established industries,
including <color=#3366CC>weaving</color>, leatherwork, <color=#3366CC>metalwork</color>, <color=#3366CC>masonry</color>, and <color=#3366CC>pottery</color>.
Some scholars contest the idea of a Proto-Euphratean language or one substrate language; they think the Sumerian
language may originally have been that of the <color=#3366CC>hunting</color> and <color=#3366CC>fishing</color> peoples who lived in the marshland and the <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>
<color=#3366CC>Arabia littoral region</color> and were part of the Arabian <color=#3366CC>bifacial</color> culture. Juris Zarins believes the Sumerians lived along the
coast of <color=#3366CC>Eastern Arabia</color>, today's <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color> region, before it was flooded at the end of <color=#3366CC>the Ice Age</color>.
Sumerian civilization took form in the <color=#3366CC>Uruk period</color> (4th millennium BC), continuing into the Jemdet Nasr and <color=#3366CC>Early</color>
<color=#3366CC>Dynastic</color> periods. The Sumerian city of <color=#3366CC>Eridu</color>, on the coast of the Persian Gulf, is considered to have been one of the
oldest cities, where three separate cultures may have fused: that of peasant Ubaidian farmers, living in mud-brick huts
and practicing irrigation; that of mobile nomadic Semitic pastoralists living in black tents and following herds of sheep
and goats; and that of fisher folk, living in reed huts in the marshlands, who may have been the ancestors of the
Sumerians.
Reliable historical records begin with Enmebaragesi (<color=#3366CC>Early Dynastic I</color>). The Sumerians progressively lost control to
Semitic states from the northwest. Sumer was conquered by the Semitic-speaking kings of the Akkadian Empire
around 2270 BC (short chronology), but Sumerian continued as a sacred language. Native Sumerian rule re-emerged
for about a century in the <color=#3366CC>Third Dynasty of Ur</color> at approximately 2100–2000 BC, but the Akkadian language also
remained in use for some time.
Archeological discovery
The Sumerians were entirely unknown during the early period of modern archeology. Jules Oppert was the first scholar
to publish the word Sumer in a lecture on 17 January 1869. The first major excavations of Sumerian cities were in 1877
at Girsu by the French archeologist Ernest de Sarzec, in 1889 at Nippur by John Punnett Peters from the <color=#3366CC>University of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Pennsylvania</color> between 1889 and 1900, and in Shuruppak by German archeologist Robert Koldewey in 1902–1903.
Major publications of these finds were "Decouvertes en Chaldée par Ernest de Sarzec" by Léon Heuzey in 1884, "Les
Inscriptions de Sumer et d'Akkad" by François Thureau-Dangin in 1905, and "Grundzüge der sumerischen Grammatik"
on Sumerian grammar by Arno Poebel in 1923.
City-states in Mesopotamia
In the late 4th millennium BC, Sumer was divided into many independent <color=#3366CC>city-states</color>, which were divided by canals and
boundary stones. Each was centered on a temple dedicated to the particular patron god or goddess of the city and
ruled over by a priestly governor (ensi) or by a king (lugal) who was intimately tied to the city's religious rites.

Apart from Mari, which lies full 330 kilometres (205 miles) north-west of Agade, but which is credited in the king list as
having exercised kingship in the Early Dynastic II period, and Nagar, an outpost, these cities are all in the
Euphrates-Tigris alluvial plain, south of <color=#3366CC>Baghdad</color> in what are now the Bābil, Diyala, Wāsit, Dhi Qar, Basra, Al-Muthannā
and Al-Qādisiyyah governorates of <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>.
History
The Sumerian city-states rose to power during the prehistoric Ubaid and Uruk periods. Sumerian written history
reaches back to the 27th century BC and before, but the historical record remains obscure until the Early Dynastic III
period, c. 23rd century BC, when the language of the written records becomes easier to decipher, which has allowed
archaeologists to read contemporary records and inscriptions.
The <color=#3366CC>Akkadian Empire</color> was the first state that successfully united larger parts of Mesopotamia in the 23rd century BC.
After the Gutian period, the <color=#3366CC>Ur III kingdom</color> similarly united parts of northern and southern Mesopotamia. It ended in the
face of <color=#3366CC>Amorite</color> incursions at the beginning of the second millennium BC. The Amorite "dynasty of Isin" persisted until c.
1700 BC, when Mesopotamia was united under <color=#3366CC>Babylonian</color> rule.
